proposal: Lassman recommends repealing the Jones Act, the 1920 law requiring ships that carry cargo between U.S. ports to be U.S.-built, U.S.-owned and U.S.-crewed, arguing it has shrunk the U.S. fleet and raised shipping costs. The next administration should unilaterally grant Jones Act exemptions wherever the law allows, as is often done in hurricane season, and work with Congress to repeal the law.

status_summary: The first half of the recommendation, exemptions where allowed, is partly met by a temporary waiver; the repeal half has not advanced. The White House announced a Jones Act waiver in March 2026 that lets foreign-flag vessels carry oil, fuel and fertilizer between U.S. ports, with the administration saying it would reduce short-term disruption in the oil market (Cato, 2026-03-18; Argus describes the issue date as 17 March and links it to a U.S.-Iran war). The waiver was extended by 90 days on 2026-04-24 (NEFI) and again: a CBP bulletin of 2026-08-13 (CSMS 69519766) says DHS approved, at the Department of War's request, a second 90-day extension effective 2026-08-17 covering products loaded before 23:59 ET on 2026-11-15, with a vessel availability request and a post-voyage report to MARAD required; trade press reports the covered product list cut from more than 600 tariff codes in April to 237 (AJOT, 2026-08-18). MARAD's domestic shipping page confirms waiver dates of 2026-03-17, 2026-05-18 and 2026-08-17 and waiver-voyage reports through October 2026. On repeal, Sen. Lee and Rep. McClintock introduced the Open America's Waters Act (S. 2043 and H.R. 3940) on 2025-06-12; GovInfo bill status shows referral to committee with no later action, no administration proposal was found, and the law remains in force. NEFI and 14 other trade associations wrote to congressional leaders on 2026-04-23 urging permanent reform, and 52 House Republicans, including the Speaker, signed a 2026-06-30 letter urging that the waiver not be renewed (Argus). No waiver document appears in a Federal Register search for the Jones Act since 2025-01-20.

timeline.event: Sen. Lee (S. 2043) and Rep. McClintock (H.R. 3940) introduce the Open America's Waters Act, described in its title as repealing the Jones Act limits on coastwise trade: it rewrites 46 U.S.C. 12112(a) so any vessel that qualifies under U.S. law may receive a coastwise endorsement, directs the Coast Guard to issue implementing regulations within 90 days, and repeals the section on loss of coastwise privileges. The bills were referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee; GovInfo bill status shows no action after referral (H.R. 3940 was referred to the Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee on 2025-06-13), and no administration endorsement was found.

A Jones Act waiver issued to the Department of War takes effect, dated 2026-03-17 (date per MARAD's domestic shipping page and the title of the later CBP guidance); MARAD's page also lists extensions dated 2026-05-18 and 2026-08-17 and posts monthly waiver-voyage reports under 46 U.S.C. 501(c), but does not state the waiver's scope or link the waiver documents.
The White House announces a 90-day extension of the waiver, moving expiry from May 17 to mid-August, citing new data that more supply reached U.S. ports faster.

CBP guidance (CSMS 69519766) says DHS approved, at the request of the Department of War, a second 90-day extension of the 2026-03-17 waiver, effective 2026-08-17 and covering products loaded before 23:59 ET on 2026-11-15, with a vessel availability request explaining the national defense purpose and a post-voyage report to MARAD required.

MARAD posts 12 waiver-voyage reports dated 2026-09-08 through 2026-09-29 under the 2026-08-17 extension, showing the waiver in use in September 2026 (the index page does not state cargo types, vessel flags or the expiry).

title: Repeal the Jones Act and use waivers and exemptions in the meantime
uncertainties: A CBP bulletin (content.govdelivery.com, 2026-08-13) confirms the issuing route (DHS approval at the Department of War's request), the 2026-08-17 effective date and the 2026-11-15 loading deadline; it requires requests to explain how each voyage serves national defense and cites 46 U.S.C. 501(c) for post-voyage reports, which is consistent with a national defense waiver under 46 U.S.C. 501(a), but the waiver's own text was not read and the product list spreadsheet was not opened. A Seafarers union post (2026-09-01) dates the second extension's issuance to 2026-08-10, which differs from the bulletin date (likely issuance versus guidance). MARAD's domestic shipping page confirms waiver dates (2026-03-17, 2026-05-18 and 2026-08-17) and voyage reports through September 2026; its 2026-05-18 extension date differs from a trade association's report of a White House announcement on 2026-04-24 (announcement versus effective date). No extension past 2026-11-15, termination or litigation was found through 2026-10-13 in one search. Repeal bills S. 2043 and H.R. 3940: GovInfo bill status, read in review on 2026-10-17, shows S. 2043 referred to Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation (2025-06-12) and H.R. 3940 referred to House Transportation and Infrastructure (2025-06-12) and its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee (2025-06-13), with no later action and no cosponsors; other Jones Act bills may exist. Cato, NEFI, AJOT and the Seafarers union take sides on Jones Act reform, and their characterizations of the waiver's effects are not adopted. The CBP bulletin, re-read in full on 2026-10-17, does not name the covered products or their count (they are in an attached spreadsheet that was not opened), so the oil, fuel and fertilizer scope and the 237-code figure rest on Cato, Argus and AJOT. Member and trade association letters are described in the summary as context and are not timeline actions.
